title: Working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms by housing tenure in a rural county
subtitle: Cross-sectional household survey with test-button verification
statement: After two carbon monoxide deaths in rented farm cottages, the county health unit does not know how many homes have a working carbon monoxide alarm or a working smoke alarm, or whether renters are worse off than owners. A cross-sectional household survey this winter would estimate the prevalence of working alarms by tenure and heating type so that the alarm giveaway can be targeted.
whoAffected: Households in a rural county of about 180,000 people, especially renters in older farm cottages heated with solid fuel or bottled gas, and the environmental health team and fire service who run the alarm programme.
whatHurts: Carbon monoxide poisoning is silent and often fatal at night; alarms that are absent, badly sited or past their replacement date give no warning. The current giveaway reaches people who ask for home visits, who may be the households least at risk.
currentPractice: Alarms are fitted during fire service home safety visits made on request; the health unit has no population estimate of working alarms and relies on an untraced figure of 40 percent.
whyNow: Two deaths last winter, pressure from the board to act before the next heating season, and a fieldwork window that closes at the end of March.
constraints: Fieldwork budget of 18,000; fieldwork ends by the end of March; entry only to the hallway or kitchen with an adult householder present; the property roll has no tenure field.
patientCenteredGoal: Every household at risk of carbon monoxide exposure has a working, correctly sited alarm before the next heating season.
summary: Problem framed as a prevalence question by tenure and heating type, to target an existing alarm programme.
